subject: psychology
topic: Bystanders step in far more often than the textbook story says
angle: While the presence of others generally reduces the likelihood of helping, real-life footage shows that the presence of danger significantly increases the likelihood of bystander intervention.
title: The truth about bystanders

hooks.text: Will you stay still or step in?
You think crowds stop help. Danger changes that.
You wait for others to act first.
A street corner. A sudden shout. A crowd.

reveal.headline: Danger makes people act.
reveal.body: Bystanders were 19 times more likely to intervene in real-life conflicts when danger was present than when it was not. The evidence is mixed.

explain.headline: The bystander effect is not absolute.
explain.body: While more people usually reduce the chance of help, this effect is smaller in dangerous situations. It weakens when the risk of physical harm is clear and the perpetrator is visible.

matters.headline: Your instinct is tied to risk.
matters.body: That may be why you feel paralyzed in a crowd of strangers, but your body might react differently if the threat becomes immediate and physical.

example.headline: A sidewalk at night.
example.body: You see a heated argument between two people under a streetlamp. You wait to see if someone else moves first. You watch their hands move toward each other's faces.

claims.text: In real-life conflicts recorded by cameras, bystanders were 19 times more likely to intervene when danger was present than when it was not.
claims.quote: In the presence of danger, bystanders were 19 times more likely to intervene than in the absence of danger.

claims.text: The bystander effect was attenuated when situations were perceived as dangerous, perpetrators were present, and the costs of intervention were physical.
claims.quote: The bystander effect was attenuated when situations were perceived as dangerous (compared with non-dangerous), perpetrators were present (compared with non-present), and the costs of intervention were physical (compared with non-physical).

claims.text: The presence of other people in a critical situation reduces the likelihood that an individual will help.
claims.quote: Research on bystander intervention has produced a great number of studies showing that the presence of other people in a critical situation reduces the likelihood that an individual will help.

verdict: The evidence shows that while the 'bystander effect' exists, it is significantly mitigated by the presence of danger and specific situational factors.
caveat: The finding that danger increases intervention is based on a specific analysis of 80 interpersonal conflicts recorded by public surveillance cameras.
caption:
The bystander effect is often taught as a rule of human behavior.

Research shows that while the presence of others generally reduces the likelihood of helping, the effect is significantly mitigated by the presence of danger.

How does your behavior change when the risk is clear?
